nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Hot, dry foothill summers and cool, snowy mountain winters set the growing season from oak woodland up to the sequoia groves.

nodes.name: Snowpack & Kaweah meltwater
nodes.desc: Most precipitation falls in winter, as heavy snow at Lodgepole elevation. Meltwater feeds the Kaweah River drainage and the forests and woodlands it crosses.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.desc: Giant sequoias are adapted to fire, which dries cones, clears rival growth and exposes bare soil. Fire suppression let fuel build up, and large recent fires burned in the groves.

nodes.name: Soil & nutrients
nodes.desc: Foothill and forest soils hold the nutrients that oaks, shrubs and sequoias draw up, replenished by fallen leaves, wood and droppings.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen needles, acorn husks, wood and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Giant sequoia
nodes.desc: The most massive single-stem tree on Earth, growing in groves such as Giant Forest at roughly 5,500 to 9,000 feet. Its cones open mainly through fire heat and insect damage.

nodes.name: Blue oak
nodes.desc: Dominant tree of the dry blue oak woodland in the Sierra foothills, alongside gray pine and other oaks. Its acorns are eaten by wildlife.

nodes.name: California black oak
nodes.desc: Links the foothill chaparral to the higher conifer forest. Its acorns are a food for deer, bears and woodpeckers.

nodes.name: Greenleaf manzanita
nodes.desc: A shrub of mid-elevation forest and chaparral whose flowers feed bumble bees and whose berries are food for wildlife.

nodes.name: Sequoia cone longhorn beetle
nodes.desc: Its larvae bore into giant sequoia cones, cutting off water to the scales so cones dry and open and release seed.

nodes.name: Douglas squirrel
nodes.desc: Strips scales off cones for the seeds and eats giant sequoia cone scales, acorns and mushrooms. Discarded scales pile up in middens.

nodes.name: Acorn woodpecker
nodes.desc: In California acorns make up half or more of its diet, which it stores in drilled granary trees, also eating sap and insects. One of the best-recorded birds near the park.

nodes.name: Mule deer
nodes.desc: Mostly browses shrubs and trees, with forbs, fruit and acorns, from the foothills to the montane forest. Main large prey of mountain lions.

nodes.name: Vosnesensky Bumble Bee
nodes.desc: The most-recorded bumble bee near the park. Forages on a range of wildflowers and shrubs and nests underground, often in rodent burrows.

nodes.name: Western Fence Lizard
nodes.desc: Eats mostly land invertebrates, mainly insects, and is an important food for snakes and birds of prey.

nodes.name: Western rattlesnake
nodes.desc: Eats small mammals, birds and reptiles; Californian snakes take more lizards than elsewhere.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: The most-recorded bird near the park, an opportunistic feeder that scavenges carrion.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: Soars over the foothills looking for carrion.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: Omnivore: mostly plants and acorns, plus insects such as bees and ants, carrion, and in spring deer fawns.

nodes.name: Mountain lion
nodes.desc: Prefers deer among large prey and takes smaller animals too. In California black bears visit many of its kills.

nodes.name: Red-tailed hawk
nodes.desc: A soaring hawk of the foothills; GloBI records show it eating lizards, rattlesnakes, ravens and woodpeckers near the park.
